{{smaller block|The question [of a state church], at the present juncture, is in itself so absolutely unimportant! ''The thing'' is, to recast religion.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Literature and Dogma, Pref.}}}}

{{smaller block|Flattered vanity was a pleasing sensation, she admitted, but tangible advantage was ''the thing'' after all.
{{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, I. v.}}}}

'''Thing-in-itself''' (translating the German ''Ding an sich''), a noumenon.—'''Thing of naught''' or '''nothing''', a thing of no value or importance; a mere nothing; a cipher.

{{smaller block|Man is like a ''thing of nought''; his time passeth away like a shadow. {{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Psalter, Ps. cxliv. 4.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Ham.'' The King is a ''thing''—
''Guil.'' A thing, my lord!
''Ham.'' ''Of nothing.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 2. 30.}}}}

'''Things in action''', legal rights to things not in the possession of the claimant.—'''To do the handsome thing by''', to treat with munificence or generosity. [Many analogous phrases are formed by the substitution of other adjectives for handsome: as, to ''do the friendly, proper, square,'' or ''right thing by'' a person.] [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|You see I'm ''doing the handsome thing by'' you, because my father knows yours.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, i. 5.}}}}

'''To know a thing or two''', to be experienced or knowing; hence, to be shrewd or sharp-witted. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|My cousin is a sharp blade, but I think I have shown him that we in Virginia ''know a thing or two''.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Virginians, xviii.}}}}

'''To make a good thing of''', to derive profit from: as, to ''make a good thing of'' stock-jobbing. [Colloq.]

'''thing<sup>2</sup>''' (ting), ''n.'' [Not from AS. ''thing'', a council, but repr. Icel. ''thing'', an assembly, confer-

too indifferent, to designate more precisely. [Colloq. or vulgar.]

{{smaller block|A lonely grey house, with a ''thingumebob'' at the top; a servatory they call it. {{right|''Bulwer'', Eugene Aram, i. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|A polyp would be a conceptual thinker if a feeling of "Hollo! ''thingumbob'' again!" ever flitted through its mind. {{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychology, I. 463.}}}}

'''thingummy''' (thing′um-i), ''n.'' [Also ''thingamy''; a capricious extension of ''thing'', as if < ''thing''<sup>1</sup> + ''-um'' (a quasi-L. term.) + ''-y''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''thingumbob''.] Same as ''thingumbob''.

{{smaller block|What a bloated aristocrat ''Thingamy'' has become since he got his place!
{{right|''Thackeray'', Character Sketches (Misc., V. 343).}}}}

{{smaller block|"And so," says Xanthias, in the slovenly jargon of gossip, "the ''thingummy'' is to come off?" "Yes," replies Aeacus in the same style, "directly; and this is where the thingumbobs are to work." {{right|''Classical Rev.'', III. 259.}}}}

'''thin-gut†''' (thin′gut), ''n.'' A starveling. [Low.]

{{smaller block|Thou ''thin-gut!''
Thou thing without moisture!
{{right|''Massinger'', Believe as you List, iii. 2. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''thin-gutted''' (thin′gut″ed), ''a.'' Having a thin, lean, or flaccid belly, as a fish.

{{smaller block|A slim ''thin-gutted'' fox. {{right|''Sir R. L'Estrange.''}}}}

'''thingy''' (thing′i), ''a.'' [< ''thing''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. Material; like a material object; objective; actual; real.—2. Materialistic; practical; given to thinginess; pragmatical: as, a ''thingy'' person or view. [Recent in both uses.]

'''think'''<sup>1</sup> (thingk), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''thought'', ppr. ''thinking''. [< ME. ''thinken'', ''thynken'', prop. ''thenken'', also assibilated ''thenchen'' (pret. ''thought'', ''thoughte'', pp. ''thought''), < AS. ''thencan'', ''thencean'' (pret. ''thohte'', pp. ''thoht'') = OS. ''thenkian'' = OFries. ''thanka'', ''thenkia'', ''tensa'' = OHG. ''denchan'', MHG. ''denken'', G. ''denken'', think, = Icel. ''thekkja'', perceive (mod. Icel. ''thenkja'' = Sw. ''tänka'' = Dan. ''tænke'', think, are influenced by the G.), = Goth. ''thagkjan'', think; connected with AS. ''thanc'', etc., thought, thank (see ''thank''); orig. factitive of a strong verb, AS. *''thincan'', pret. *''thanc'', pp. *''thuncen'', which appears only in the secondary form, ''thyncan'' (pret. ''thūhte'', etc.), seem: see ''think''<sup>2</sup>, which has been more or less confused with ''think''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. OL. ''tongere'', know, ''tongitio''(''n''-), knowing. For the relation of the mod. form ''think''<sup>1</sup> to AS. ''thencan'', cf. that of ''drink'' and ''drench''<sup>1</sup> to AS. ''drencan'', and of ''sink'', tr., to AS. ''sencan''.] I. ''trans.'' 1. To judge; say to one's self mentally; form as a judgment or conception.

{{smaller block|'Twere damnation
To ''think'' so base a thought.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 7. 50.}}}}

{{smaller block|Again ''thought'' he, Since heretofore I have made a conquest of angels, shall Great-heart make me afraid?
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|"What a noble heart that man has," she ''thought''.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, lxvi.}}}}

2. To form a mental image of; imagine: often equivalent to recollect; recall; consider.

{{smaller block|"''Thenke'','' quod the Iewe, "what I thee dede
When thou was with vs in that stede."
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 92.}} Ther nas no man so wys that koude ''thenche''
So gay a popelote, or swich a wenche.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller's Tale, l. 67.}}}}

{{smaller block|Vlfyn that is wise and a trewe knyght hath ordeyned all this pees, and the beste ordenaunce that eny can ''thynke.'' {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 80.}}}}

{{smaller block|If parts allure thee, ''think'' how Bacon shined,
The wisest, brightest, meanest of mankind.
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, iv. 281.}}}}

3. To cognize; apprehend; grasp intellectually.

{{smaller block|The animal perceives no "object," no "causal nexus," not being able to form such abstractions from his feelings. If man is gifted with another power, and ''thinks'' an "object" or a "causal nexus," it is because he can detach and fix in signs, rendering explicit what is implicit in feeling. ''G. H. Lewes'', Probs. of Life and Mind, II. iii. § 5.}}

{{smaller block|We ''think'' the ocean as a whole by multiplying mentally the impression we get at any moment when at sea.
{{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychology, II. 203.}}}}

4. To judge problematically; form a conception of (something) in the mind and recognize it as possibly true, without decidedly assenting to it as such.

{{smaller block|Charity . . . ''thinketh'' no evil [taketh not account of evil, R. V.]. {{right|1 Cor. xiii. 5.}}}}

{{smaller block|He sleeps and ''thinks'' no harme.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii., Con.}}}}

5. To purpose; intend; mean; contemplate; have in mind (to do): usually followed by an infinitive clause as the object.

{{smaller block|When he seid all that he ''thought'' to seye,
Ther nedid noo displeasur to be sought.
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 204.}}}}

{{smaller block|No hurte to me they ''thinke.''
{{right|''Taming of a Shrew'' (Child's Ballads, VIII. 184).}}}}

{{smaller block|I ''think'' not to rest till I come thither.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 20.}}}}

{{smaller block|Many of the colonists at Boston ''thought'' to remove, or did remove, to England.
{{right|''Emerson'', Hist. Discourse at Concord.}}}}

6. To hold as a belief or opinion; opine; believe; consider.

{{smaller block|The better gowns they have on, the better men they ''think'' themselves. In the which thing they do twice err; for they be no less deceived in that they ''think'' their gown the better than they be in that they ''think'' themselves the better.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Thinking'' vs enemies, [they] sought the best aduantage they could to fight with vs.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, II. 227.}}}}

{{smaller block|Besides, you are a Woman; you must never speak what you ''think''.
{{right|''Congreve'', Love for Love, ii. 11.}}}}

7. To feel: as, to ''think'' scorn. [Obsolete or provincial.]

{{smaller block|Loue lelli what thou louest al mi lif dawes,
& hate heiȝeli in hert that thou hate ''thenkest''.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4720.}}}}

{{smaller block|Scho fand all wrang that sould bene richt,
I trow the man ''thought'' richt grit schame.
{{right|''Wyf of Auchtirmuchty'' (Child's Ballads, VIII. 121).}}}}

8. To modify (an immediate object of cognition) at will; operate on by thought (in a specified way).

{{smaller block|Meditation here
May ''think'' down hours to moments.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, vi. 85.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
